text:
Which condition must be satisfied for an object to perform simple harmonic motion?

A. The acceleration is constant in magnitude and directed towards the equilibrium position.
B. The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and directed towards the equilibrium position.
C. The velocity is proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and directed away from the equilibrium position.
D. The restoring force is constant in magnitude and always opposite to the velocity.
ms: **B.** SHM is defined by $a \propto -x$: the acceleration is proportional to displacement and always directed towards equilibrium. A describes a constant restoring acceleration (not SHM); C confuses velocity with acceleration; D describes a constant force such as friction.

text:
A simple pendulum of length $L$ has period $T$ on Earth, where the gravitational field strength is $g$. A second simple pendulum of length $2L$ oscillates on a planet where the gravitational field strength is $2g$. What is the period of the second pendulum?

A. $2T$
B. $\sqrt{2}\,T$
C. $\dfrac{T}{2}$
D. $T$
ms: **D.** $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ depends on $L/g$, and $\dfrac{2L}{2g} = \dfrac{L}{g}$, so the period is unchanged. B comes from changing only $L$; A from treating $T$ as proportional to $\sqrt{Lg}$; C from treating $T \propto 1/g$ only.

text:
An object performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude $0.040\ \text{m}$ and period $0.50\ \text{s}$. What is the maximum speed of the object?

A. $0.080\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
B. $0.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
C. $0.50\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
D. $6.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
ms: **C.** $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = 12.6\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ and $v_{\max} = \omega x_0 = 12.6 \times 0.040 = 0.50\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. A is $x_0/T$ (no $2\pi$); B uses $\omega = \pi/T$; D is the maximum acceleration $\omega^2 x_0$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

text:
An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude $x_0$. What fraction of the total energy of the oscillation is kinetic energy when the displacement is $\dfrac{x_0}{2}$?

A. $\dfrac{1}{4}$
B. $\dfrac{1}{2}$
C. $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
D. $\dfrac{3}{4}$
ms: **D.** $E_K = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_0^2 - x^2)$ and $E_T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$, so $\dfrac{E_K}{E_T} = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{x_0^2} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$. A is the fraction that is potential energy; B assumes energy varies linearly with displacement; C is the ratio of the speed to the maximum speed.

text:
The graph shows how the displacement of an object performing simple harmonic motion varies with time.

![displacement-time graph with points P, Q, R, S](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.1_5.svg)

At which point does the object have its maximum velocity in the positive direction?

A. P
B. Q
C. R
D. S
ms: **D.** Velocity is the gradient of the displacement–time graph. At S the graph crosses zero with the steepest positive gradient. At P (and R) the gradient is zero; at Q the speed is maximum but the velocity is negative. R is where the acceleration is maximum and positive.

text:
A student investigates how the period $T$ of a mass–spring oscillator depends on the mass $m$ attached to the spring. For each mass, the time $t_{10}$ for 10 complete oscillations is measured with a stopwatch. (Illustrative data.)

| $m$ / kg | $t_{10}$ / s | $T^2$ / $\text{s}^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.100 | 3.98 | 0.158 |
| 0.200 | 5.60 | 0.314 |
| 0.300 | 6.91 | |
| 0.400 | 7.93 | 0.629 |
| 0.500 | 8.90 | 0.792 |

(a) Suggest why the student timed 10 oscillations rather than one. [1]

(b) (i) Calculate the missing value of $T^2$ for $m = 0.300\ \text{kg}$. [1]

(ii) The uncertainty in each value of $t_{10}$ is $\pm 0.1\ \text{s}$. Determine the absolute uncertainty in $T^2$ for $m = 0.300\ \text{kg}$. [2]

(c) The graph shows the data with the line of best fit.

![graph of T squared against m with line of best fit](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.1_6.svg)

The period is given by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$. Determine, using the graph, the spring constant $k$. [3]

(d) Another student repeats the experiment with a much heavier spring. Their graph is a straight line with the same gradient but with a positive intercept on the $T^2$ axis. Suggest why there is an intercept, and explain whether this affects the value of $k$ determined. [2]
ms:
(a)
- reduces the percentage/fractional uncertainty in $T$ (reaction time error is shared over 10 periods) ✓

(b)(i)
- $T = 0.691\ \text{s}$ so $T^2 = 0.477\ \text{s}^2$ ✓ Accept 0.478

(b)(ii)
- fractional uncertainty in $T$ = $\dfrac{0.1}{6.91} = 1.4\%$ and fractional uncertainty in $T^2$ = $2 \times 1.4\% = 2.9\%$ ✓
- $\Delta(T^2) = 0.029 \times 0.477 = \pm 0.014\ \text{s}^2$ ✓ Accept $\pm 0.01\ \text{s}^2$

(c)
- gradient from the line using two well-separated points, e.g. $\dfrac{0.79 - 0.16}{0.50 - 0.10} \approx 1.6\ \text{s}^2\ \text{kg}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 1.5–1.7
- gradient $= \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}$ ✓
- $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{1.6} \approx 25\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 23–26 $\text{N m}^{-1}$; allow ECF from their gradient

(d)
- (part of) the mass of the spring also oscillates, so the effective oscillating mass is greater than $m$ ✓ Accept: $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}(m + m_{\text{eff}})$
- $k$ depends only on the gradient, which is unchanged, so $k$ is not affected ✓

text:
A block of mass $0.25\ \text{kg}$ rests on a frictionless horizontal surface and is attached to a spring of spring constant $40\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. The block is displaced $0.030\ \text{m}$ from its equilibrium position and released.

(a) Outline why the block performs simple harmonic motion. [2]

(b) Calculate the period of oscillation of the block. [2]

(c) Sketch a graph showing how the acceleration $a$ of the block varies with its displacement $x$ between $x = -0.030\ \text{m}$ and $x = +0.030\ \text{m}$. Label the values of $a$ at the end points. [2]

(d) The block is now displaced $0.060\ \text{m}$ and released. State and explain the effect on the period. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the restoring force from the spring is $F = -kx$, proportional to the displacement ✓
- so the acceleration $a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$ is proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position ✓

(b)
- $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.25}{40}}$ ✓
- $T = 0.50\ \text{s}$ ✓ Accept 0.497 s

(c)
- straight line through the origin with negative gradient ✓
- end points at $(-0.030,\ +4.8)$ and $(+0.030,\ -4.8)$ with $a$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓

![expected sketch: straight line of negative gradient through origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.1_7.svg)

(d)
- period is unchanged ✓
- the period depends only on $m$ and $k$ / the oscillation is isochronous: $T$ is independent of amplitude ✓

text:
A simple pendulum consists of a small bob on a light inextensible string.

(a) State one condition necessary for the pendulum to perform approximately simple harmonic motion. [1]

(b) Calculate the length of the string needed for the pendulum to have a period of $2.00\ \text{s}$ at a place where $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. [2]

(c) The same pendulum is taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is $1.62\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$. Calculate its period on the Moon. [2]

(d) The bob is released from rest at one extreme position. Describe the energy changes of the bob as it moves to the other extreme position. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the amplitude/angular displacement is small (less than about $10°$) ✓ Accept air resistance negligible / string light and inextensible

(b)
- $L = \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{9.81 \times 2.00^2}{4\pi^2}$ ✓
- $L = 0.994\ \text{m}$ ✓ Accept 0.99 m

(c)
- $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.994}{1.62}}$ ✓ Accept $T = 2.00\sqrt{9.81/1.62}$
- $T = 4.92\ \text{s}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (b)

(d)
- gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy as the bob falls, kinetic energy is maximum at the lowest point/equilibrium position ✓
- kinetic energy is transferred back to gravitational potential energy as it rises to the other extreme, where it is momentarily at rest; total energy constant (if air resistance negligible) ✓

text:
An object of mass $0.20\ \text{kg}$ attached to a horizontal spring oscillates with simple harmonic motion on a frictionless surface. The amplitude is $0.060\ \text{m}$ and the frequency is $2.5\ \text{Hz}$. At time $t = 0$ the object is at its maximum positive displacement.

(a) Show that the angular frequency of the oscillation is about $16\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. [1]

(b) Calculate the maximum acceleration of the object. [2]

(c) Calculate the speed of the object when its displacement is $0.030\ \text{m}$. [2]

(d) Calculate the total energy of the oscillation. [2]

(e) Determine the shortest time after $t = 0$ at which the displacement of the object is $0.030\ \text{m}$. [2]

(f) State the frequency at which the kinetic energy of the object varies, explaining your answer. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 2.5 = 15.7\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓ (AG: about 16)

(b)
- $a_{\max} = \omega^2 x_0 = 15.7^2 \times 0.060$ ✓
- $a_{\max} = 14.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓ Accept 15 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ (using $\omega = 16$ gives 15.4)

(c)
- $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2} = 15.7\sqrt{0.060^2 - 0.030^2}$ ✓
- $v = 0.82\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 0.83 using $\omega = 16$

(d)
- $E_T = \tfrac{1}{2} m\omega^2 x_0^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.20 \times 15.7^2 \times 0.060^2$ ✓
- $E_T = 0.089\ \text{J}$ ✓ Accept 0.089–0.092 J

(e)
- $x = x_0\cos\omega t$ so $0.030 = 0.060\cos(15.7t)$, giving $\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ✓
- $t = \dfrac{\pi/3}{15.7} = 0.067\ \text{s}$ ✓ Accept $T/6 = 0.067$ s; do not award if calculator in degree mode gives an answer

(f)
- $5.0\ \text{Hz}$ ✓
- kinetic energy is maximum twice in each oscillation (at equilibrium moving in each direction) / $E_K \propto \sin^2\omega t$, which has half the period ✓

text:
A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of $95\ \text{MHz}$. What is the wavelength of the radio waves in air?

A. $0.32\ \text{m}$
B. $3.2\ \text{m}$
C. $32\ \text{m}$
D. $2.9 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m}$
ms: **B.** $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^8}{95 \times 10^6} = 3.2\ \text{m}$. A and C are power-of-ten errors with the mega prefix; D comes from multiplying $c$ by $f$.

text:
Three waves are listed.

I. a sound wave in air
II. a wave on a spring produced by pushing one end backwards and forwards along the axis of the spring
III. light from a lamp

Which are longitudinal waves?

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** In sound and in the spring pushed along its axis, the particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer (longitudinal). Light is an electromagnetic wave, which is transverse, so any option containing III is wrong.

text:
The graph shows the displacement of the particles of a medium against distance along a travelling wave at one instant. The speed of the wave is $2.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

![displacement-distance graph of a travelling wave](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.2_3.svg)

What is the period of the wave?

A. $0.17\ \text{s}$
B. $1.9\ \text{s}$
C. $3.0\ \text{s}$
D. $0.33\ \text{s}$
ms: **D.** From the graph $\lambda = 0.80\ \text{m}$, so $T = \dfrac{\lambda}{v} = \dfrac{0.80}{2.4} = 0.33\ \text{s}$. A uses $\lambda = 0.40\ \text{m}$ (half a wavelength); B is $\lambda v$; C is $v/\lambda$, the frequency in Hz.

text:
A longitudinal wave travels to the right through a medium. The graph shows, at one instant, the displacement of particles against their equilibrium positions. A displacement to the right is positive.

![displacement against equilibrium position for a longitudinal wave with points P, Q, R, S](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.2_4.svg)

Which point is at the centre of a compression?

A. P
B. Q
C. R
D. S
ms: **B.** At Q the displacement is zero; particles just to the left of Q have positive displacement (moved right, towards Q) and particles just to the right have negative displacement (moved left, towards Q), so particles crowd together at Q. At S the particles on either side move away from S (rarefaction). P and R are particles with maximum displacement, which are at normal spacing — a common error is to think the crest of the graph is a compression.

text:
A transverse wave of wavelength $0.80\ \text{m}$ travels along a rope. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of two points on the rope that are $0.20\ \text{m}$ apart along the direction of travel?

A. $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\ \text{rad}$
B. $\pi\ \text{rad}$
C. $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \text{rad}$
D. $8\pi\ \text{rad}$
ms: **C.** Phase difference $= \dfrac{2\pi \Delta x}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 0.20}{0.80} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. A omits the factor 2; B would need a separation of half a wavelength; D inverts the ratio.

text:
Which statement is true for all electromagnetic waves travelling in a vacuum?

A. They travel at the same speed.
B. They have the same frequency.
C. They are longitudinal waves.
D. They have the same wavelength.
ms: **A.** All electromagnetic waves travel at $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum. Frequency and wavelength differ across the spectrum (B, D), and electromagnetic waves are transverse (C).

text:
Water waves of frequency $5.0\ \text{Hz}$ are produced in a ripple tank. A student changes the depth $d$ of the water and measures the wavelength $\lambda$ of the waves each time. (Illustrative data.)

| $d$ / cm | $\lambda$ / cm | $v$ / $\text{m s}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 4.4 | 0.220 |
| 1.0 | 6.3 | 0.315 |
| 1.5 | 7.7 | |
| 2.0 | 8.9 | 0.445 |
| 2.5 | 9.9 | 0.495 |

(a) Calculate the wave speed $v$ for a depth of $1.5\ \text{cm}$. [1]

(b) For shallow water, theory predicts that $v = \sqrt{gd}$. The graph shows $v^2$ plotted against $d$ with a line of best fit.

![graph of v squared against depth with line of best fit](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.2_7.svg)

Determine, using the graph, a value for $g$. [3]

(c) In a different tank, waves pass from a deep region into a shallow region. The frequency of the waves does not change. Explain, with reference to the data, what happens to the wavelength of the waves. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $v = f\lambda = 5.0 \times 0.077 = 0.385\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 0.39

(b)
- $v^2 = gd$ so the gradient of the graph equals $g$ ✓
- gradient calculated from the line using two well-separated points, e.g. $\dfrac{0.25 - 0.05}{0.025 - 0.005}$ ✓
- $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓ Accept 9.4–10.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$

(c)
- the data show that the wave speed decreases as the depth decreases ✓
- since $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$ and $f$ is constant, the wavelength decreases ✓

text:
A tuning fork produces a sound of frequency $512\ \text{Hz}$ in air. The speed of sound in air is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Describe the nature of a sound wave in air. [2]

(b) Calculate the wavelength of the sound. [1]

(c) Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave. [2]

(d) Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum. [1]
ms:
(a)
- longitudinal wave: air molecules oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer ✓
- producing a series of compressions and rarefactions (regions of high and low pressure) ✓

(b)
- $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{512} = 0.664\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- in a transverse wave the particles/field oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer ✓
- in a longitudinal wave the particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer ✓

(d)
- sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles/a medium to oscillate and pass on the disturbance; a vacuum has none ✓

text:
A transverse wave travels along a long string in the positive $x$ direction. Graph 1 shows the displacement of the string against distance $x$ at time $t = 0$.

Graph 1:

![graph 1: displacement against distance at t = 0, point P marked](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.2_9.svg)

Graph 2 shows how the displacement of one particle of the string varies with time.

Graph 2:

![graph 2: displacement against time for one particle](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.2_9-2.svg)

(a) State the amplitude and the wavelength of the wave. [2]

(b) Calculate the speed of the wave. [2]

(c) State and explain the direction of motion of the particle at P at $t = 0$. [2]

(d) State the phase difference between the particles at $x = 0.30\ \text{m}$ and $x = 0.90\ \text{m}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- amplitude = $15\ \text{mm}$ ✓
- wavelength = $1.2\ \text{m}$ ✓

(b)
- from graph 2, $T = 40\ \text{ms}$ so $f = 25\ \text{Hz}$ ✓
- $v = f\lambda = 25 \times 1.2 = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a)

(c)
- upwards / in the positive displacement direction ✓
- as the wave moves to the right, the crest at $x = 0.30\ \text{m}$ moves towards P, so P's displacement is about to increase / P takes the displacement of the part of the string to its left ✓ Award the second mark only with a correct direction

(d)
- $\pi$ rad / $180°$ / antiphase ✓

text:
An earthquake produces two types of wave that travel through the Earth: P-waves and S-waves. In the region considered, P-waves travel at $7.5\ \text{km s}^{-1}$ and S-waves travel at $4.0\ \text{km s}^{-1}$. (Illustrative data.)

(a) P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse. Distinguish between these two types of wave in terms of the direction of oscillation of the particles of the medium. [2]

(b) At a seismometer, the P-waves arrive $52\ \text{s}$ before the S-waves. Determine the distance from the seismometer to the source of the earthquake. Assume both waves travel in straight lines at constant speed. [3]

(c) Seismometers on the opposite side of the Earth to an earthquake detect P-waves but not S-waves. Suggest what this indicates about the outer core of the Earth. [2]

(d) A P-wave has a frequency of $2.0\ \text{Hz}$. Calculate its wavelength. [1]
ms:
(a)
- longitudinal (P): particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer/propagation ✓
- transverse (S): particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer/propagation ✓

(b)
- $\dfrac{d}{4.0} - \dfrac{d}{7.5} = 52$ ✓
- $d\left(0.250 - 0.133\right) = 52$ ✓
- $d = 446\ \text{km}$ ✓ Accept 450 km / $4.5 \times 10^5\ \text{m}$. Award [3] for a correct final answer

(c)
- transverse waves cannot travel through liquids (a liquid cannot support a shear/sideways restoring force) ✓
- so the outer core is liquid ✓

(d)
- $\lambda = \dfrac{7.5}{2.0} = 3.75\ \text{km}$ / $3.8 \times 10^3\ \text{m}$ ✓

text:
A ray of light travels from air into glass of refractive index $1.50$. The angle of incidence is $40°$. What is the angle of refraction?

A. $25°$
B. $27°$
C. $60°$
D. $75°$
ms: **A.** $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 40°}{1.50} = 0.429$, so $r = 25.4° \approx 25°$. B divides the angle itself by 1.50; C multiplies the angle by 1.50; D uses $\sin r = 1.50 \sin 40°$ (inverting the ratio).

text:
Light travels in glass of refractive index $1.60$ towards a boundary with water of refractive index $1.33$. What is the critical angle at the glass–water boundary?

A. $39°$
B. $49°$
C. $56°$
D. Total internal reflection cannot occur at this boundary.
ms: **C.** $n_1 \sin c = n_2 \sin 90°$ so $\sin c = \dfrac{1.33}{1.60} = 0.831$ and $c = 56°$. A is the critical angle for glass–air and B for water–air. D is wrong because light is travelling from the higher to the lower refractive index, so total internal reflection is possible.

text:
Water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. Which describes the changes to the frequency, speed and wavelength of the waves?

A. frequency unchanged, speed decreases, wavelength increases
B. frequency decreases, speed decreases, wavelength unchanged
C. frequency unchanged, speed increases, wavelength increases
D. frequency unchanged, speed decreases, wavelength decreases
ms: **D.** Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction. Waves travel more slowly in shallow water, and since $\lambda = v/f$ the wavelength decreases. B wrongly lets the frequency change; A and C are inconsistent with $v = f\lambda$ or with the slower speed in shallow water.

text:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$ is incident on two narrow slits separated by $0.30\ \text{mm}$. Interference fringes are observed on a screen $2.0\ \text{m}$ from the slits. What is the separation of adjacent bright fringes?

A. $0.40\ \text{mm}$
B. $4.0\ \text{mm}$
C. $2.0\ \text{mm}$
D. $40\ \text{mm}$
ms: **B.** $s = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 2.0}{0.30 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$. A and D are power-of-ten errors in converting nm and mm; C is the distance from a bright fringe to the adjacent dark fringe.

text:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $500\ \text{nm}$ is incident normally on a diffraction grating that has $600$ lines per millimetre. What is the total number of bright maxima that can be observed?

A. $3$
B. $4$
C. $6$
D. $7$
ms: **D.** $d = \dfrac{1}{600}\ \text{mm} = 1.67 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}$; $\sin\theta \le 1$ gives $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = 3.3$, so the highest order is $n = 3$. There are orders 1, 2, 3 on each side plus the central (zero-order) maximum: $2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$. A is only the highest order; C forgets the central maximum; B counts the maxima on one side only plus the central maximum.

text:
Monochromatic light passes through a single slit of width $b$ and the angular width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is $\theta$. The slit width is reduced to $\dfrac{b}{2}$. Assume small angles. What is the new angular width of the central maximum?

A. $\dfrac{\theta}{4}$
B. $\dfrac{\theta}{2}$
C. $2\theta$
D. $4\theta$
ms: **C.** The first minimum is at $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so the angular width of the central maximum ($2\theta_1$) is inversely proportional to $b$: halving $b$ doubles it. B assumes the width is proportional to $b$; A and D wrongly square the factor.

text:
A student uses a laser and a double slit of slit separation $d = 0.25\ \text{mm}$ to measure the wavelength of laser light. The distance $D$ from the slits to the screen is varied and, for each value of $D$, the width $w$ across 10 fringe separations is measured. (Illustrative data.)

| $D$ / m | $w$ / mm | $s$ / mm |
|---|---|---|
| 1.00 | 21.0 | 2.10 |
| 1.50 | 32.2 | 3.22 |
| 2.00 | 42.4 | |
| 2.50 | 53.5 | 5.35 |
| 3.00 | 63.6 | 6.36 |

(a) Suggest why the student measured across 10 fringe separations rather than one. [1]

(b) Calculate the fringe separation $s$ for $D = 2.00\ \text{m}$. [1]

(c) The graph shows $s$ against $D$ with a line of best fit.

![graph of fringe separation against D with line of best fit](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.3_7.svg)

Determine, using the graph, the wavelength of the laser light. [3]

(d) The uncertainty in $d$ is $\pm 0.01\ \text{mm}$. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the wavelength due to the uncertainty in $d$ alone. [1]

(e) The laser is replaced by one that emits light of a shorter wavelength. State and explain the effect on the gradient of the graph. [2]
ms:
(a)
- reduces the percentage uncertainty in $s$ (fringe edges are hard to locate; the error is spread over 10 separations) ✓

(b)
- $s = 4.24\ \text{mm}$ ✓

(c)
- gradient = $\dfrac{\lambda}{d}$ ✓
- gradient from the line ≈ $2.13 \times 10^{-3}$ (2.13 mm per m, a dimensionless ratio) ✓ Accept 2.0–2.2 $\times 10^{-3}$
- $\lambda = 2.13 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.25 \times 10^{-3} = 5.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ (530 nm) ✓ Accept 500–550 nm; allow ECF from gradient. Unit conversion must be correct

(d)
- $\dfrac{0.01}{0.25} \times 100 = 4\%$ ✓

(e)
- the gradient decreases ✓
- gradient $= \dfrac{\lambda}{d}$ (from $s = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$) and $d$ is unchanged, so the gradient is proportional to $\lambda$ / fringes are closer together at every $D$ ✓

text:
A ray of monochromatic light is incident on a rectangular glass block in air. The angle of incidence is $50°$ and the angle of refraction in the glass is $30°$.

![ray passing through a rectangular glass block, angles 50 degrees and 30 degrees to the normal](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.3_8.svg)

(a) Calculate the refractive index of the glass. [2]

(b) Calculate the speed of light in the glass. [2]

(c) Explain why the ray that emerges from the lower face of the block is parallel to the incident ray. [2]

(d) The wavelength of the light in air is $633\ \text{nm}$. Calculate its wavelength in the glass. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $n = \dfrac{\sin 50°}{\sin 30°}$ ✓
- $n = 1.53$ ✓

(b)
- $v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^8}{1.53}$ ✓
- $v = 1.96 \times 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a)

(c)
- the faces are parallel, so the angle of incidence at the lower face equals the angle of refraction at the upper face ($30°$) ✓
- applying Snell's law in reverse, the ray emerges at $50°$ to the normal, the same as the incident angle, so it is parallel (but laterally displaced) ✓

(d)
- $\lambda_{\text{glass}} = \dfrac{633}{1.53} = 413\ \text{nm}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a)

text:
The diagram shows plane wavefronts of water waves in a ripple tank approaching a gap in a barrier. The width of the gap is approximately equal to the wavelength.

![plane wavefronts approaching a gap in a barrier](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.3_9.svg)

(a) Sketch the shape of three wavefronts after they have passed through the gap. [2]

(b) State the effect on the spreading of the waves if the gap is made much wider than the wavelength. [1]

(c) The barrier is removed. Two dippers, vibrating in phase at $12\ \text{Hz}$, produce waves that travel at $0.24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. A point P on the water surface is $0.170\ \text{m}$ from one dipper and $0.200\ \text{m}$ from the other. Determine whether P is a point of maximum or minimum disturbance. [3]

(d) Explain why a stable interference pattern is only observed if the two sources are coherent. [2]
ms:
(a)
- wavefronts spread out as (approximately) semicircular arcs centred on the gap ✓
- wavelength (spacing between wavefronts) unchanged ✓

(b)
- the waves spread out (diffract) much less / only slightly at the edges ✓

(c)
- $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{0.24}{12} = 0.020\ \text{m}$ ✓
- path difference $= 0.200 - 0.170 = 0.030\ \text{m} = 1.5\lambda$ ✓
- path difference is a half-integer number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in antiphase and P is a minimum ✓ Do not award the final mark without the reasoning

(d)
- coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference ✓
- so the phase difference at each point stays constant and the positions of the maxima and minima do not change / with varying phase difference the pattern would shift rapidly and average out ✓

text:
An optical fibre has a core of refractive index $1.52$ surrounded by cladding of refractive index $1.46$. A ray of light enters the flat end of the fibre from air at an angle $\theta$ to the axis of the fibre, as shown.

![ray entering an optical fibre at angle theta and reflecting at the core-cladding boundary](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.3_10.svg)

(a) State two conditions required for total internal reflection to occur. [2]

(b) Calculate the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary. [2]

(c) Determine the maximum value of $\theta$ for which the ray is totally internally reflected at the core–cladding boundary. [3]

(d) Suggest one reason why the core is surrounded by cladding rather than air. [1]
ms:
(a)
- light travels from a medium of higher refractive index towards one of lower refractive index ✓
- the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle ✓

(b)
- $\sin c = \dfrac{1.46}{1.52}$ ✓
- $c = 73.8°$ ✓

(c)
- angle of refraction at the end face $= 90° - 73.8° = 16.2°$ ✓ Allow ECF from (b)
- $\sin\theta = 1.52 \sin 16.2°$ ✓
- $\theta = 25°$ ✓ Award [3] for a correct final answer

(d)
- protects the core surface from scratches/dirt that would cause light to escape / prevents light passing between touching fibres / reduces the range of angles and so reduces multipath (modal) dispersion ✓

text:
(a) Light of wavelength $633\ \text{nm}$ is incident normally on a diffraction grating with $500$ lines per millimetre.

(i) Calculate the angle between the second-order maximum and the central maximum. [2]

(ii) Determine the highest order of maximum that can be observed. [2]

(b) The grating is replaced by a double slit with the same slit separation. Compare the pattern produced by the double slit with the pattern produced by the grating. [2]

(c) A different double slit has slits of width $0.040\ \text{mm}$ separated by $0.20\ \text{mm}$. It is illuminated with light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$ and the pattern is observed on a screen $1.5\ \text{m}$ away. The graph shows how the intensity varies with position on the screen.

![double-slit intensity pattern modulated by a single-slit envelope](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.3_11.svg)

(i) State the number of bright fringes within the central maximum of the single-slit envelope. [1]

(ii) Explain why there is no bright fringe at a position $22.5\ \text{mm}$ from the centre of the pattern. [2]
ms:
(a)(i)
- $d = \dfrac{1}{500}\ \text{mm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}$ and $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2 \times 633 \times 10^{-9}}{2.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.633$ ✓
- $\theta = 39°$ ✓ Accept 39.3°

(a)(ii)
- $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{633 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.2$ ✓
- highest order is $n = 3$ ✓ Do not accept 4

(b)
- the maxima are in the same positions/angles ✓
- the grating maxima are much narrower/sharper and brighter (with darker regions between them) ✓

(c)(i)
- 9 ✓ (central fringe plus orders 1 to 4 on each side)

(c)(ii)
- the first minimum of single-slit diffraction is at $x = \dfrac{\lambda D}{b} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.5}{0.040 \times 10^{-3}} = 22.5\ \text{mm}$ ✓
- this coincides with the fifth-order double-slit maximum ($5 \times \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = 5 \times 4.5\ \text{mm}$), so the single-slit envelope is zero there and that fringe is missing ✓

text:
A standing wave is formed on a string. The wavelength of the travelling waves that form it is $\lambda$. What is the distance between two adjacent nodes?

A. $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$
B. $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$
C. $\lambda$
D. $2\lambda$
ms: **B.** Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart. A is the node-to-adjacent-antinode distance; C is the distance between alternate nodes.

text:
A string of length $0.90\ \text{m}$ is fixed at both ends. The diagram shows the standing wave on the string. The speed of waves on the string is $180\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

![standing wave with three loops on a string of length 0.90 m](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.4_2.svg)

What is the frequency of vibration?

A. $100\ \text{Hz}$
B. $200\ \text{Hz}$
C. $600\ \text{Hz}$
D. $300\ \text{Hz}$
ms: **D.** Three loops means $L = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}$, so $\lambda = 0.60\ \text{m}$ and $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{180}{0.60} = 300\ \text{Hz}$. A is the fundamental frequency; B takes $\lambda = L$; C takes $\lambda = L/3$ (counting each loop as a wavelength).

text:
A pipe of length $0.34\ \text{m}$ is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air in the pipe is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. End effects are negligible. Which frequency is **not** a resonant frequency of the air in the pipe?

A. $750\ \text{Hz}$
B. $1250\ \text{Hz}$
C. $500\ \text{Hz}$
D. $250\ \text{Hz}$
ms: **C.** For a pipe closed at one end the fundamental has $\lambda = 4L = 1.36\ \text{m}$, so $f_1 = 250\ \text{Hz}$, and only odd harmonics occur: 250, 750, 1250 Hz, ... 500 Hz would be the second harmonic, which would be possible for a pipe open at both ends but not for a closed pipe.

text:
A lightly damped system is driven by a periodic force of variable frequency. The amount of damping is then increased. What happens to the maximum amplitude of the system and to the shape of the resonance curve?

A. maximum amplitude decreases, peak becomes broader
B. maximum amplitude decreases, peak becomes sharper
C. maximum amplitude increases, peak becomes broader
D. maximum amplitude unchanged, peak becomes broader
ms: **A.** Greater damping removes more energy per cycle, so the amplitude at resonance is smaller and the response is spread over a wider range of driving frequencies (a broader, flatter peak; the peak also shifts slightly to lower frequency). B gives the effect of reducing damping on the shape; C and D ignore the energy dissipated.

text:
Two successive resonant frequencies of the air column in a pipe are $450\ \text{Hz}$ and $750\ \text{Hz}$. No other resonant frequency lies between them. What type of pipe is it, and what is its fundamental frequency?

A. open at both ends, $300\ \text{Hz}$
B. open at both ends, $150\ \text{Hz}$
C. closed at one end, $150\ \text{Hz}$
D. closed at one end, $300\ \text{Hz}$
ms: **C.** For a pipe open at both ends successive harmonics differ by $f_1$, giving $f_1 = 300\ \text{Hz}$, but 450 Hz is not a whole-number multiple of 300 Hz, so A is impossible. For a pipe closed at one end successive (odd) harmonics differ by $2f_1$, so $f_1 = 150\ \text{Hz}$ and $450 = 3f_1$, $750 = 5f_1$. B would make 600 Hz a resonance between them; D takes the difference as $f_1$.

text:
A student investigates resonance in a tube closed at its lower end by water. A vibrating tuning fork is held above the open end and the length $L$ of the air column is increased from zero until the first (loudest) resonance is heard. This is repeated with tuning forks of different frequency $f$. (Illustrative data.)

| $f$ / Hz | 256 | 288 | 320 | 384 | 480 | 512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $L$ / cm | 32.4 | 28.5 | 25.7 | 21.0 | 16.7 | 15.5 |

(a) Explain why a loud sound is heard only at particular lengths of the air column. [2]

(b) Because the antinode at the open end is slightly outside the tube, the relationship is $L + e = \dfrac{v}{4f}$, where $e$ is the end correction and $v$ is the speed of sound. The graph shows $L$ against $\dfrac{1}{f}$ with a line of best fit.

![graph of L against 1/f with line of best fit](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.4_6.svg)

Determine, using the graph, the speed of sound in the tube. [3]

(c) Determine the end correction $e$. [1]

(d) Predict the length of the air column at which the next resonance occurs with the $512\ \text{Hz}$ tuning fork. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the sound wave reflects at the water surface and superposes with the incident wave to form a standing wave ✓
- resonance (loud sound) occurs only when the length allows a node at the water surface and an antinode at the open end, i.e. when the natural frequency of the air column equals the fork frequency ✓

(b)
- gradient $= \dfrac{v}{4}$ ✓
- gradient from the line ≈ $\dfrac{(32.4 - 15.5) \times 10^{-2}}{(3.91 - 1.95) \times 10^{-3}} \approx 86\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 83–89 $\text{m s}^{-1}$; must convert cm to m
- $v = 4 \times \text{gradient} \approx 345\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 330–355; allow ECF from gradient

(c)
- intercept on the $L$ axis is $-e$, so $e \approx 1.3\ \text{cm}$ ✓ Accept 0.8–1.8 cm

(d)
- next resonance when $L + e = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}$, with $\dfrac{\lambda}{4} = 15.5 + e \approx 16.8\ \text{cm}$ ✓
- $L = 3 \times 16.8 - 1.3 \approx 49\ \text{cm}$ ✓ Accept 48–50 cm; Accept $L_2 = L_1 + \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$; allow ECF from (b) and (c)

text:
A guitar string of length $0.65\ \text{m}$ is fixed at both ends. When plucked, it vibrates in its first harmonic with a frequency of $196\ \text{Hz}$.

(a) Describe how a standing wave is formed on the string. [2]

(b) Calculate the speed of the waves on the string. [2]

(c) The guitarist presses the string against the neck so that the vibrating length is reduced to $0.49\ \text{m}$. The tension is unchanged. Calculate the new frequency of the first harmonic. [2]

(d) State two differences between a standing wave and a travelling wave. [2]
ms:
(a)
- waves travel along the string and are reflected at the fixed ends ✓
- two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose / interfere ✓

(b)
- first harmonic: $\lambda = 2L = 1.30\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $v = f\lambda = 196 \times 1.30 = 255\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(c)
- wave speed unchanged, new $\lambda = 0.98\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $f = \dfrac{255}{0.98} = 260\ \text{Hz}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (b)

(d) Any two of:
- a standing wave does not transfer energy along the string; a travelling wave does ✓
- amplitude varies with position (zero at nodes, maximum at antinodes) in a standing wave; constant for a travelling wave ✓
- all points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase (and in antiphase with the next segment) in a standing wave; phase changes continuously with position in a travelling wave ✓

text:
The diagram shows a pipe of length $0.85\ \text{m}$ that is open at both ends. The speed of sound in air is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. End effects are negligible.

![pipe of length 0.85 m open at both ends](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.4_8.svg)

(a) Sketch, on a copy of the diagram, the standing wave pattern of displacement for the first harmonic. Label the positions of any nodes (N) and antinodes (A). [2]

(b) Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic. [2]

(c) One end of the pipe is now closed. Determine the frequencies of the three lowest harmonics that can now be produced. [3]

(d) The temperature of the air in the open pipe increases, so the speed of sound increases. State the effect on the frequency of the first harmonic. [1]
ms:
(a)
- displacement antinodes (A) at both open ends ✓
- a single node (N) at the centre, with the envelope drawn as two curves crossing there ✓

(b)
- $\lambda = 2L = 1.70\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $f = \dfrac{340}{1.70} = 200\ \text{Hz}$ ✓

(c)
- closed pipe: $\lambda = 4L = 3.40\ \text{m}$, fundamental $= 100\ \text{Hz}$ ✓
- only odd harmonics are possible ✓
- $100\ \text{Hz}$, $300\ \text{Hz}$, $500\ \text{Hz}$ ✓ Do not award the final mark if 200 Hz is included

(d)
- the frequency increases (wavelength is fixed by the pipe, and $f = v/\lambda$) ✓

text:
A mass of $0.50\ \text{kg}$ hangs from a spring. The top of the spring is driven up and down by an oscillator of variable frequency. The graph shows how the amplitude of oscillation of the mass varies with the driving frequency. The system is lightly damped.

![resonance curve: amplitude against driving frequency](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.4_9.svg)

(a) Distinguish between the natural frequency of the system and the driving frequency. [2]

(b) Using the graph, estimate the spring constant of the spring. [2]

(c) Sketch, on a copy of the graph, the curve you would expect if the damping were increased. [2]

(d) The suspension of a car consists of springs and shock absorbers. Explain why the suspension is designed to be close to critically damped. [2]
ms:
(a)
- natural frequency: the frequency at which the system oscillates when displaced and left to oscillate freely ✓
- driving frequency: the frequency of the external periodic force applied to the system ✓

(b)
- resonance (maximum amplitude) at about $2.0\ \text{Hz}$, which is (approximately) the natural frequency ✓
- $k = 4\pi^2 f^2 m = 4\pi^2 \times 2.0^2 \times 0.50 = 79\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 75–82

(c)
- lower peak amplitude at all frequencies (curve below original everywhere) ✓
- broader peak, with the maximum at the same or a slightly lower frequency ✓

(d)
- after hitting a bump the car body returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time ✓
- without oscillating/bouncing (underdamped would oscillate; overdamped would return too slowly and fail to absorb the next bump) ✓

text:
The diagram shows wavefronts emitted by a source of sound S that is moving at constant velocity. W, X, Y and Z are stationary observers.

![wavefronts from a moving source S with observers W, X, Y and Z](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.5_1.svg)

Which observer detects the highest frequency?

A. W
B. X
C. Y
D. Z
ms: **A.** The source moves towards W (the arrow and the crowding of wavefronts on the right), so the wavefronts reaching W are closest together: shortest wavelength and highest frequency. Y is behind the source and detects the lowest frequency; X and Z are roughly perpendicular to the motion and detect nearly the emitted frequency.

text:
A spectral line of hydrogen has a wavelength of $656.3\ \text{nm}$ when measured in the laboratory. In the spectrum of a distant galaxy the same line is observed at $662.9\ \text{nm}$. What is the speed of the galaxy relative to Earth, and its direction of motion?

A. $3.0 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards Earth
B. $3.0 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from Earth
C. $3.0 \times 10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from Earth
D. $3.0 \times 10^7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from Earth
ms: **B.** $v \approx \dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}c = \dfrac{6.6}{656.3} \times 3.00 \times 10^8 = 3.0 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The observed wavelength is longer (red shift), so the galaxy is moving away. A has the wrong direction; C and D are power-of-ten errors.

text:
A source emitting sound of frequency $500\ \text{Hz}$ moves directly towards a stationary observer at $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The speed of sound in air is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What frequency does the observer detect?

A. $459\ \text{Hz}$
B. $500\ \text{Hz}$
C. $544\ \text{Hz}$
D. $548\ \text{Hz}$
ms: **D.** For a moving source $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v - u_s} = 500 \times \dfrac{340}{310} = 548\ \text{Hz}$. A is the frequency for a source moving away; C uses the moving-observer equation $f\dfrac{v + u_o}{v}$; B ignores the Doppler effect.

text:
A source emits sound of frequency $1000\ \text{Hz}$. The speed of sound is $v$.

Situation 1: the source moves at $0.10v$ directly towards a stationary observer.
Situation 2: the observer moves at $0.10v$ directly towards a stationary source.

What are the frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ detected by the observer in situations 1 and 2?

A. $f_1 = 1100\ \text{Hz}$, $f_2 = 1100\ \text{Hz}$
B. $f_1 = 1111\ \text{Hz}$, $f_2 = 1100\ \text{Hz}$
C. $f_1 = 1100\ \text{Hz}$, $f_2 = 1111\ \text{Hz}$
D. $f_1 = 1111\ \text{Hz}$, $f_2 = 1111\ \text{Hz}$
ms: **B.** Moving source: $f_1 = \dfrac{1000\,v}{v - 0.10v} = \dfrac{1000}{0.90} = 1111\ \text{Hz}$. Moving observer: $f_2 = \dfrac{1000\,(v + 0.10v)}{v} = 1100\ \text{Hz}$. The two situations are not symmetrical because the motion relative to the medium matters; A and D assume they are, and C swaps the equations.

text:
A calcium absorption line has a wavelength of $393.4\ \text{nm}$ when measured in the laboratory. The table shows the wavelength $\lambda_{\text{obs}}$ of this line observed in the spectra of five galaxies, A–E, and their distances from Earth. (Illustrative data.)

| galaxy | distance / Mpc | $\lambda_{\text{obs}}$ / nm |
|---|---|---|
| A | 20 | 395.2 |
| B | 45 | 397.5 |
| C | 80 | 400.7 |
| D | 120 | 404.4 |
| E | 160 | 408.1 |

(a) Calculate, in $\text{km s}^{-1}$, the speed of galaxy C relative to Earth. [2]

(b) The graph shows the speeds of the galaxies plotted against their distances, with a line of best fit through the origin.

![graph of recession speed against distance with line through origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_C.5_5.svg)

Determine the gradient of the line, including its unit. [2]

(c) Suggest why the equation $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \dfrac{v}{c}$ is appropriate for these galaxies. [1]

(d) State what the data indicate about the direction of motion of the galaxies relative to Earth. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $\Delta\lambda = 400.7 - 393.4 = 7.3\ \text{nm}$ and $v = \dfrac{7.3}{393.4} \times 3.00 \times 10^5$ ✓
- $v = 5.6 \times 10^3\ \text{km s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 5570 km s⁻¹; accept $5.6 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ only if the unit is stated

(b)
- value from the line, e.g. $\dfrac{11.2 \times 10^3}{160} \approx 70$ ✓ Accept 66–74
- unit $\text{km s}^{-1}\ \text{Mpc}^{-1}$ ✓

(c)
- the speeds are much less than the speed of light ($v/c$ is at most about 0.04) ✓

(d)
- all the lines are red-shifted (longer wavelength), so all the galaxies are moving away from Earth ✓

text:
(a) An ambulance with its siren sounding moves at constant speed along a straight road towards a stationary pedestrian. Explain, with reference to wavefronts, why the pedestrian hears a higher frequency than the frequency emitted by the siren. [3]

(b) State what is meant by the term red shift when applied to light from a star. [1]

(c) A spectral line has a wavelength of $486.1\ \text{nm}$ when measured in the laboratory. The same line in the spectrum of a star is observed at $485.4\ \text{nm}$. Determine the speed of the star relative to Earth and state its direction of motion. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the siren emits wavefronts at regular time intervals, each centred on the position of the source when it was emitted ✓
- because the source moves towards the pedestrian between emissions, the wavefronts in front of it are closer together, so the observed wavelength is shorter ✓
- the speed of sound is unchanged, so more wavefronts reach the pedestrian per second / $f = v/\lambda$ is higher ✓

(b)
- an increase in the observed wavelength (decrease in frequency) of light because the source is moving away from the observer ✓

(c)
- $v = \dfrac{0.7}{486.1} \times 3.00 \times 10^8 = 4.3 \times 10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept $4 \times 10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
- moving towards Earth (blue shift: observed wavelength shorter) ✓

text:
A bat flies at $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ directly towards a large flat wall. It emits ultrasound of frequency $40.0\ \text{kHz}$, which reflects from the wall back to the bat. The speed of sound in air is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Explain why the frequency of the ultrasound received at the wall is greater than $40.0\ \text{kHz}$. [2]

(b) Calculate the frequency of the ultrasound received at the wall. [2]

(c) The wall reflects the ultrasound without changing its frequency. Calculate the frequency of the reflected ultrasound detected by the bat. [2]

(d) Suggest how the bat could use the difference between the emitted and detected frequencies to judge its speed relative to the wall. [1]
ms:
(a)
- the bat (source) moves towards the wall between emitting successive wavefronts ✓
- so the wavefronts arriving at the wall are closer together/shorter wavelength, and with the same wave speed the frequency is higher ✓

(b)
- moving source: $f' = 40.0 \times \dfrac{340}{340 - 5.0}$ ✓
- $f' = 40.6\ \text{kHz}$ ✓ Accept 40.6 kHz

(c)
- the wall acts as a stationary source of frequency $f'$ and the bat is an observer moving towards it: $f'' = f'\dfrac{340 + 5.0}{340}$ ✓
- $f'' = 41.2\ \text{kHz}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (b). Award [1] max if the moving-source equation is used again for the reflected wave (the numerical answer is similar, but the method is wrong)

(d)
- the frequency difference increases with speed (approximately proportional to it, $\Delta f \approx 2uf/v$), so a larger shift means a higher closing speed ✓

text:
A train sounds its horn continuously as it travels at constant speed along a straight track past a stationary observer on a platform. As the train approaches, the observer hears a frequency of $580\ \text{Hz}$. After the train has passed, the observer hears a frequency of $500\ \text{Hz}$. The speed of sound is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Describe how the frequency heard by the observer changes as the train approaches, passes and moves away. [2]

(b) Show that the speed of the train is about $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. [3]

(c) Calculate the frequency emitted by the horn. [1]
ms:
(a)
- the frequency heard is (approximately) constant at 580 Hz, higher than the emitted frequency, while the train approaches at constant speed ✓
- it falls rapidly as the train passes the observer, then remains (approximately) constant at 500 Hz, lower than the emitted frequency, as it recedes ✓ Accept a correctly described or sketched frequency–time graph

(b)
- $580 = f\dfrac{340}{340 - u}$ and $500 = f\dfrac{340}{340 + u}$ ✓
- dividing: $\dfrac{580}{500} = \dfrac{340 + u}{340 - u}$ ✓
- $u = \dfrac{0.16 \times 340}{2.16} = 25.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ (AG)

(c)
- $f = 580 \times \dfrac{340 - 25.2}{340} = 537\ \text{Hz}$ ✓ Accept 536–538 Hz
